lessons: Define the decision before gathering evidence.
Write the investment thesis in falsifiable terms.
Separate observed facts from estimates and opinions.
Ask how each source is rewarded and constrained.
Prefer primary evidence over repeated commentary.
Record the date attached to every important fact.
Use only information available at the decision date.
Standardize accounting definitions before comparing businesses.
Reconcile reported earnings with actual cash generation.
Judge earnings quality, not merely earnings growth.
Trace working-capital changes through the cash flow statement.
Treat recurring one-time charges as recurring costs.
Measure dilution on a per-share basis.
Read the balance sheet before forecasting the income statement.
Map debt maturities, covenants, and refinancing needs.
Test liquidity under adverse operating conditions.
Look for obligations that sit outside headline debt.
Distinguish cyclical improvement from structural progress.
Normalize margins across a full business cycle.
Verify unit economics before extrapolating growth.
Identify whether growth comes from price, volume, mix, or acquisition.
Estimate how long attractive reinvestment opportunities can persist.
Focus on returns on incremental capital.
Measure customer concentration and switching risk.
Assess dependence on critical suppliers and inputs.
Look for demonstrated pricing power, not claimed pricing power.
Study competitors as carefully as the target.
Consider substitution from outside the defined industry.
Demand evidence that a moat protects economic returns.
Treat regulation as both a constraint and a competitive variable.
Align management incentives with per-share value creation.
Evaluate capital allocation through completed actions.
Interpret insider transactions in context, not isolation.
Treat guidance as evidence, not as a forecast substitute.
Analyze segment economics before valuing the whole.
Separate geographic growth from currency translation.
Model material currency exposures explicitly.
Use sustainable tax rates rather than convenient ones.
Include pension and benefit obligations in economic leverage.
Treat stock-based compensation as a real expense.
Value the business under several coherent scenarios.
Use ranges when the inputs do not justify precision.
Reverse-engineer the expectations embedded in the price.
Match the discount rate to the risks of the cash flows.
Make terminal assumptions economically defensible.
Choose comparables for economic similarity, not ticker familiarity.
Relate valuation multiples to growth, durability, and risk.
Estimate expected return, not just upside to a target.
Start with relevant base rates before embracing a special story.
Balance the inside view with the outside view.
Build the bear case before committing capital.
Run a pre-mortem and name plausible failure paths.
Search deliberately for evidence that could disprove the thesis.
State the strongest opposing argument fairly.
Identify what you believe that the market does not.
Measure consensus before claiming a variant view.
Do not confuse a catalyst with fundamental value.
Be humble about timing even when direction seems clear.
Model the path, not only the destination.
Match the investment horizon to the liability horizon.
Size positions by downside, uncertainty, and correlation.
Risk only capital whose loss you can tolerate.
Let concentration be earned by evidence and resilience.
Assume correlations can rise during stress.
Use leverage only after modeling forced-sale risk.
Require a margin of safety against estimation error.
Prefer favorable asymmetry to impressive point forecasts.
Ask how the investment recovers after the downside case.
Distinguish permanent impairment from temporary volatility.
Set decision rules before emotions become involved.
Predefine thesis-breaking evidence and kill criteria.
Use a checklist for recurring analytical errors.
Keep a decision journal with reasons and expectations.
Timestamp forecasts so hindsight cannot rewrite them.
Attach calibrated confidence levels to key judgments.
Update beliefs in proportion to the strength of new evidence.
Do not move the goalposts to protect a favored thesis.
Ignore sunk research costs when reassessing an investment.
Evaluate process separately from outcome.
Separate skill from luck across many decisions.
Respect sample size before drawing conclusions.
Check for survivorship bias in every historical comparison.
Look for selection bias in datasets and anecdotes.
Prevent look-ahead bias in backtests and case studies.
Penalize complex models for overfitting risk.
Test which assumptions actually drive the conclusion.
Make calculations reproducible by another careful reader.
Audit formulas, links, units, and signs.
Use consistent units and denominators throughout analysis.
Verify crucial numbers through an independent route.
Treat stale data as a source of hidden risk.
Do not mistake decimal precision for knowledge.
Document missing data instead of silently filling gaps.
Make uncertainty explicit in both analysis and sizing.
Distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence.
Prefer explanatory power over narrative appeal.
If the thesis cannot be explained simply, refine it.
Write the causal chain from action to cash flow.
Consider second-order effects and competitor responses.
Map incentives for every important stakeholder.
Use channel checks as samples, not universal truths.
Treat expert opinion as input, not authority.
Do not trade on rumors you cannot verify.
Match the frequency of information to the investment horizon.
Protect attention from news that cannot change the decision.
Compare every opportunity with the best available alternative.
Include opportunity cost in every hold decision.
Use cash or a low-risk benchmark as a real alternative.
Include taxes, fees, spreads, and market impact.
Recognize that turnover compounds friction.
Test whether the strategy can be implemented as modeled.
Account for capacity before scaling a successful approach.
Plan entry and exit conditions before taking the position.
Assess crowding through ownership, positioning, and shared assumptions.
Monitor leading indicators tied directly to the thesis.
Schedule reviews instead of reacting to every price move.
Archive the original thesis before revising it.
Admit errors early, clearly, and without euphemism.
Change a decision when the evidence changes, not when pride permits.
Protect intellectual integrity; its returns compound.
